Chapel
chăp´ěl
n. (a sanctuary held by a king; Amaziah's name for the shrine at Bethel)
From Late Latin cappella, the shrine housing St Martin's cloak. The KJV uses it once, at Amos 7:13, for Hebrew miqdash melek — the king's sanctuary. The translators' word carries exactly the sense: a holy place that belongs to a man.

Biblical Definition

Amaziah the priest of Bethel tries to expel Amos with an argument about ownership: “But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court” (Amos 7:13). Every word of it is true and it proves the opposite of what he intends. Bethel was the king's — Jeroboam had made it: “Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). A sanctuary that belongs to a king is a sanctuary God did not command, and the whole indictment of the northern kingdom follows from it. Amos answers by denying that he holds any office Amaziah can revoke: “Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit” (Amos 7:14); and by naming the only commission that matters: “And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel” (Amos 7:15). A herdman with a word from God outranks a priest with a royal chapel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a chapel as a house for public worship; a private oratory; or a place of worship subordinate to a church — and gives the origin in the cappella that housed St Martin's cloak.

expand to see more

CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; appropriately, a house for public worship subordinate to a church.

CHAPEL, n. A chapel of ease is a chapel built for the accommodation of a parish, in addition to the principal church.

CHAPEL, n. A private oratory, or place of worship in a palace or great house.

SANCTUARY, n. [L. sanctuarium, from sanctus, sacred.] A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, called the Holy of Holies.

ORATORY, n. A place destined for prayer; a closet or chapel for private devotions.

Key Scripture

Amos 7:13 — "But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court."

1 Kings 12:28 — "Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt."

Amos 7:14 — "Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:"

Amos 7:15 — "And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel."

Modern Corruption

A house of worship becomes a possession — a king's, a donor's, a founder's — and the owner then claims the right to decide what may be preached in it.

expand to see more

Amaziah's sentence is the permanent temptation of institutional religion, and it does not require a monarchy. Wherever a pulpit is owned — by the family that built the building, by the giver who underwrites the budget, by a board that treats the preacher as staff — the argument from Amos 7:13 is available and will be used. Note that Amaziah does not say Amos is wrong. He says Amos is out of bounds, which is a cheaper and far more effective objection, and one that never has to engage a text.

Jeroboam's calves show the root. He built a convenient sanctuary for a plausible reason — Jerusalem was far, and the journey was a burden — and 1 Kings 12:28 records the pitch in his own words. Worship shaped to what the people will find manageable is the beginning of the king's chapel, and the regulative principle exists to close that door: in corporate worship, what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. Amos 7:14 is the answer of a free church to an owned one. The herdman held no office Amaziah could take away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew miqdash (H4720), sanctuary, holy place; melek (H4428), king; bayith mamlakah (H1004 + H4467), a royal house, the king's court.

expand to see more

Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — a sanctuary; Amos 7:13, rendered chapel because it is the king's.

Hebrew melek (H4428) — king; the possessive that damns the shrine.

Hebrew Beth-el (H1008) — house of God; the name Jacob gave it, kept over a calf.

Hebrew noqed (H5349) — a sheep-breeder, herdman; Amos's trade, Amos 1:1 and 7:14.

Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take; Amos 7:15, the LORD took me as I followed the flock.

Usage

"“It is the king's chapel” — true, and the whole indictment."

"“It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem” — convenience, offered as mercy."

"“The LORD took me as I followed the flock” — the only commission that cannot be revoked."
